reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Caused by Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, a Gram-positive bacillus widely distributed in animals, fish and shellfish, and acquired through occupational skin inoculation
Typically affects butchers, abattoir workers, fishermen, fish handlers and veterinarians, so an occupational history is central to recognition

The usual localised cutaneous form appears after a short incubation of about 1-4 days as a well-demarcated, violaceous, painful and often intensely itchy plaque, characteristically on a finger or hand
The lesion tends to spread slowly at its advancing edge while clearing centrally and is not usually associated with suppuration or systemic upset
A rarer diffuse cutaneous form with more widespread skin involvement and a serious systemic form with bacteraemia and endocarditis also occur
The organism has a notable propensity to cause endocarditis, which may affect previously normal valves, so unexplained bacteraemia warrants echocardiography
Penicillin-class agents are highly active and are first-line; importantly the organism is intrinsically resistant to vancomycin, a key point when treating suspected bacteraemia empirically
reference.pathophysiology: Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae is introduced through minor cuts or abrasions during handling of contaminated animal or fish products. In the localised form it multiplies in the dermis, producing a slowly advancing inflammatory plaque with the characteristic violaceous colour and central clearing, generally without pus formation. In susceptible hosts the organism can invade the bloodstream, and its ability to adhere to and colonise cardiac valve endothelium underlies its striking tendency to cause endocarditis, sometimes on structurally normal valves, with the potential for systemic embolic and destructive valvular complications.
additionalDifferentials: Erysipelas or cellulitis due to streptococci or staphylococci
Gout or acute inflammatory arthritis of a digit
additionalInvestigations: Culture of a full-thickness skin biopsy from the advancing edge of the lesion (surface swabs are often unrewarding)
Blood cultures where systemic infection or endocarditis is suspected
Echocardiography, including transoesophageal study, in bacteraemic patients
Gram stain of biopsy material showing Gram-positive bacilli
Inflammatory markers to gauge severity of invasive disease
redFlags: New or changing murmur, embolic phenomena or heart failure suggesting endocarditis
Fever and systemic toxicity indicating invasive rather than localised disease
Rapidly spreading or diffuse skin involvement
Sepsis in an occupationally exposed patient
Empirical use of vancomycin, which is ineffective, in suspected Erysipelothrix bacteraemia
reference.prognosis: The localised cutaneous form is self-limiting and resolves within a few weeks, and responds promptly to penicillin; invasive disease and endocarditis carry a much more serious prognosis and require prolonged intravenous therapy and sometimes valve surgery.
pitfalls: Missing the occupational exposure and misdiagnosing the plaque as ordinary cellulitis
Relying on surface swabs rather than a deep biopsy for culture
Choosing empirical vancomycin, to which the organism is intrinsically resistant
Failing to investigate for endocarditis when bacteraemia is documented
Assuming all cases are trivial and overlooking the diffuse and systemic forms
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Penicillin as the antimicrobial of choice for the localised cutaneous form, with a cephalosporin, ciprofloxacin, clindamycin or a macrolide for penicillin-allergic patients
Avoidance of empirical vancomycin, to which Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae is intrinsically resistant
Wound care and analgesia for the painful violaceous plaque, which is usually self-limiting
Blood cultures and echocardiography, including a transoesophageal study, where bacteraemia or endocarditis is suspected
Prolonged intravenous penicillin for invasive disease and endocarditis, with valve surgery where the valve is destroyed or vegetations are large
Occupational preventive advice on protective gloves and hand hygiene when handling animal, fish or shellfish products to prevent recurrence
